disease_info: Delusional disorder is characterized by one or more persistent delusions lasting at least a month (often many months or years) in the absence of prominent hallucinations, disorganized thought, or marked negative symptoms, and with relatively preserved overall functioning outside the delusional themes. The delusions are fixed false beliefs that remain resistant to clear contradictory evidence and are not better explained by mood episodes, substance use, or another psychotic disorder. Content can involve persecution, jealousy, somatic concerns, grandiosity, or erotomanic ideas, and behavior may be subtly shaped by these beliefs while still appearing outwardly organized. Onset is often insidious in mid to later adulthood, and patients frequently present only after family, employers, or legal systems become involved because the person does not recognize the beliefs as pathological.

narrative.stressor: About a year before presentation, Nguyen led a high‑visibility cloud migration project where a series of minor outages drew intense scrutiny from management and online client forums. Around this time, he began fixating on a belief that a competing tech team within the company was covertly sabotaging his code and monitoring his personal accounts, initially channeling the concern into exhaustive log‑checking and late‑night "hardening" work. Over the next nine months, his conviction solidified despite repeated internal audits showing no anomalies, and he started avoiding collaboration, refusing to share documentation, and skipping hackathons and social basketball games to "stay ahead" of the perceived threat. The situation came to a head when HR intervened after he accused a colleague of spying during a sprint review; at the urging of his manager and a trusted cousin from Little Saigon, Nguyen reluctantly agreed to see a psychiatrist as a condition for remaining on the project.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m here because nobody seems to take it seriously that people at work are secretly targeting my projects, even when I show them the evidence.”

narrative.stressor: Peggy’s difficulties emerged gradually after a tense period in her marriage when she and her husband were juggling college costs for their eldest child and caring for her aging mother. A minor billing discrepancy at work, which was quickly corrected, seemed to trigger a growing preoccupation that certain members of her church circle and even her sister‑in‑law were quietly orchestrating situations to undermine her reputation as "honest with money." Over nine months, she increasingly interpreted missed invitations, casual comments at potlucks, and small errors in the office as part of a coordinated effort against her, though she continued to perform her job and household roles with outward competence. When she confronted a longtime friend at the library about being part of this supposed scheme and the friend tearfully suggested she talk to a doctor, Peggy—torn between her conviction and her desire to keep the peace—agreed to see a psychiatrist at her pastor’s recommendation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like certain people in my family and church are quietly working together against me, and no one believes me when I say it.”

narrative.stressor: Allen’s problems became noticeable after he developed chronic shoulder pain that limited his welding work and kept him from his usual fishing and woodworking, leaving him spending long evenings alone in his workshop and online. Following a routine imaging study that showed only mild degenerative changes, he became convinced that the clinic had concealed a serious implant or device placed in his body without consent, and he began poring over technical manuals and internet forums to "prove" it. Over the next nine months, his belief hardened despite repeated reassurances from different physicians, leading him to refuse recommended physical therapy, cancel a planned Canadian fishing trip, and start modifying metal tools and building contraptions in his shed to "detect" the supposed device. After he angrily demanded that a local surgeon remove the non‑existent implant and threatened to expose a "cover‑up" at the hospital, his wife—worried about his escalating preoccupation and withdrawal from family life—insisted he see a psychiatrist before any further medical appointments.
narrative.chief_complaint: “The doctors keep telling me nothing is there, but I know they put something inside me and they’re hiding it.”
